tob-0004-d1: This Chinese text — 人間樂 (Renjian Le), by Tianhuazangzhuren — is a work of classical Chinese literature. Its title speaks of joy in the human world. The text preserves a voice from China’s literary past. It awaits fuller study by scholars of Chinese letters.
tob-0005-d1: The Professional Approach — by Charles Harness and Theodore Thomas — is a science fiction story from the genre’s golden age. Its title promises a tale of expertise under pressure. The story represents mid-century American SF. It preserves a voice from the pulp era.
tob-0006-d1: Edward Eggleston’s Mystery of Metropolisville is a novel of small-town American life in the nineteenth century. The Indiana author wrote with humor and affection for his characters. The book captures the Midwest of his era. It remains a charming period piece.
tob-0015-d1: The Pastor of Hermas — in the Roberts and Donaldson translation — is the beloved early Christian allegory of the Shepherd, with visions, mandates, and parables. This second-century work nearly entered the New Testament canon. The text shows the primitive church’s moral teaching.
tob-0022-d1: Eunice Fuller’s Book of Friendly Giants — 1914 — retells the old giant tales for children, from Jack the Giant-Killer to the giants of Norse myth. Her warm retellings charmed young readers. The book is a delightful piece of children’s folklore.
tob-0038-d1: Church Committee Book I — Foreign and Military Intelligence — is the Senate’s landmark 1975 report on CIA assassination plots and covert action abroad. The investigation exposed decades of secret abuses. The report remains the essential record of intelligence overreach.
tob-0039-d1: This microfilm roll holds part of the court record of the Nuremberg Doctors’ Trial — the 1946-47 case against Nazi doctors for cruel medical tests on prisoners. Witnesses speak and lawyers argue in the official record. The trial gave the world the Nuremberg Code.
tob-0169-d1: James Allen’s As a Man Thinketh — 1903 — is the beloved essay on the power of thought, teaching that mind shapes character and circumstance. Its plain wisdom made it a New Thought classic. The book remains one of the most-read self-help works.
tob-0190-d1: The Sacred Writings, Volume II — from the Harvard Classics — gathers scriptures of the world’s religions, edited by Charles W. Eliot. This volume continues the five-foot shelf’s survey of faith. The collection introduced the world’s religions to American readers.
tob-0194-d1: James Christie’s Disquisition upon Etruscan Vases is an early study of the painted vases then called Etruscan — now known to be Greek. The antiquarian’s work belongs to the dawn of classical archaeology. The book is a curious relic of early scholarship.
tob-10008-d1: Edward Fairfax Taylor’s verse translation of Virgil’s Æneid brings Rome’s great epic to English readers. Aeneas’s journey from Troy to Italy unfolds in English verse. The translation belongs to the tradition of English Virgil. The epic remains the cornerstone of Latin literature.
tob-10032-d1: Virgil’s Bucolics and Eclogues gather his ten shepherd poems — songs of love and loss in an idealized countryside. These early poems founded a whole Western literary kind. The book shows Virgil before the Æneid. It remains the model all later shepherd poetry follows.
tob-10034-d1: James Rhoades’s Englishing of Virgil’s Georgics gives the great tilling-poem in verse — four books on tilth, trees, kine, and bees. Maecenas bade him sing the Italian farm back to life. The poem is the crown of Latin teaching-verse. The rendering bears Virgil’s field-music to English readers.
tob-10041-d1: W. C. Firebaugh’s 1922 Satyricon gives Petronius’s racy Roman novel in English — Trimalchio’s feast and the scrapes of Encolpius. Only fragments live on, but they glitter. The broken satire is our liveliest look at Nero’s Rome. The version brings its rude wit to English readers.
tob-10047-d1: Arthur Mee’s World’s Greatest Books — book one, tales — strings the masterpieces of world story-telling in short readable shape. The editor’s famed run bore great letters to busy Edwardian readers. The volume is a charming door to the classics.
tob-10051-d1: The whole King James Bible — the 1611 Authorized Writ — is the most weighty English book ever printed. Its saws and cadences shaped the tongue these four hundred years. This printing gives the full canon, Old and New Testaments.
tob-10102-d1: Livy’s Rome-Story — books one to eight — spans the town’s founding through the young commonwealth, from Romulus to the Samnite wars. His pages made Romans proud of their past. The great Augustus-day story-teller wrote with fatherland high-heartedness. The books stay the classic tale of early Rome.
tob-10110-d1: D. W. Culp’s Black American Letters musters the race’s writing at the twentieth century’s dawn. Its voices speak with pride and purpose. The editor gathered lays, tales, and think-pieces by the foremost race men and women. The book is a landmark of black American bookdom.
tob-10173-d1: Hosea Ballou’s Letters for God’s Open Writ plead the All-Savers’ case against the day’s doubters. His mild Universalism won thousands of hearers. The New England God-teacher upheld revelation with plain homely rede. The book is a classic of young American All-Saver thought.
tob-10175-d1: Arthur Conan Doyle’s Micah Clarke — 1889 — is his tale of Monmouth’s rising in 1685, told by a Puritan man-at-arms. Stevenson praised it above his other romances. The young Doyle penned it with love-tale heartiness. The book stays the best of his bygone-day stories.
tob-10198-d1: Terence’s Play-Books give the six living plays of Rome’s great merry-maker — Andria, Eunuchus, Heauton, and the rest. Caesar called him half a Menander. His trim Latin shaped merry-making letters two thousand years. The plays stay the model of Roman New Comedy.
tob-10200-d1: Charles Darwin’s Kinds’ Beginnings — 1859 — is the book that changed beast-lore for good, setting forth kind-shaping by picking. One book, and the world thought anew. His heedful pleading re-shaped science and man-thought. The work stays the ground of latter-day beast-lore.
tob-10228-d1: Edith Wharton’s Ethan Frome — 1911 — is the stark New England short-tale of a poor tiller caught betwixt a sickly wife and a banned love. Its famed sled-ride ending is not to be forgotten. The book stays Wharton’s most flawless short sorrow-tale.
tob-10337-d1: P. Le Page Renouf’s Englishing of the Egyptian Dead-Book gives the great burial writ — the soul’s dreadful fare-spells. The Ani papyrus is its most famous text. His scholar’s version served Victorian readers. The book opened Egypt’s afterworld to the English-speaking world.
tob-10375-d1: Walt Whitman’s Whole Prose Writings string his lays of thought, memories, Specimen Days, and Folk-Vistas — the good gray poet’s unvers’d work. His prose matches his verse in heartiness and folk high-mindedness. The gathering is needful for all Whitman lovers.
tob-10543-d1: Sir John Malcolm’s Sikh Sketch — 1812 — is the trail-blazing British tale of the Sikh folk, their story, and their faith. Ranjit Singh’s court received him with honor. The soldier-bookman wrote from eye-witness in the Punjab. The book founded western knowledge of Sikhdom.
tob-10544-d1: John Peter Arendzen’s Babylonia is the early 1900s muster of olden Babel — its story, worship, and delved ruins. The priest-bookman wrote with clearness and learning for common readers. The book is a sound door to olden river-land. Its god-lore rede stays useful.
tob-10560-d1: Anna Botsford Comstock’s Nature-Study Handbook — 1911 — is the classic teacher-and-mother’s guide, with lessons on plants, beasts, stones, and sky. Generations learned the outdoors from her pages. Her Cornell-grounded toil shaped American nature-teaching. The book stays the bible of nature-study.
tob-10562-d1: Benjamin Franklin’s book on lightning-lore strings his famed Philadelphia tryings — the kite, the lightning-rod, and his one-fluid rede. He snatched lightning from the sky, they said. His letters to London’s Royal Fellowship grounded the new science. The book is a landmark of the Lightening.
tob-10566-d1: Ambrose Bierce’s Wonder-Fables are his biting small satires — short tales with stinging morals, Aesop grown throughly sour. The Devil’s Word-Book man penned them with unmatched tooth. The gathering is a gem of dark American wit. Each fable lands like a slap.
tob-10573-d1: Clement of Alexandria’s Writings — book one of two — gives the great teacher’s Call to the Greeks and the Tutor. His school taught the faith to thinkers. The 100s father’s works bridge Greek thought and Christian faith. The volume is needful for early church students.
tob-10577-d1: Archbishop William Wake’s Barred Gospels and Letters of the first New Testament muster the cast-out writ — the banned gospels and letters. His 1693 Englishing opened the forbidden books to our readers. The gathering stays a folk classic. It has never been out of print.
tob-10580-d1: T. K. Cheyne’s Job and Solomon — Or, the Old Testament’s Wisdom — strings Job, Proverbs, and the Preacher. The sufferer’s questions still pierce the heart. The Oxford scholar’s work opened the wisdom writ to latter-day readers. The book is a fair door to bible wisdom.
tob-10592-d1: Walter W. Skeat’s Notes on Chaucer’s Canterbury Tales — on the Canon’s Yeoman’s Tale — unfold Chaucer’s keen mock of gold-lore. The Yeoman’s master proves a cheating quack. The great word-scholar’s notes unpack the Middle English for latter-day readers. The work serves all Tale students.
tob-10601-d1: Erasmus Darwin’s Beast-Lore — book two — sets out the laws of breathing life, with his trail-blazing kind-shaping rede. Charles Darwin’s famed grandsire fore-guessed picking by decades. The work is a landmark of ere-Darwin beast-lore. Song and science mingle in its leaves.
tob-10614-d1: T. Edward Bowdich’s Faring from Cape Coast Castle to Ashantee tells the 1817 British word-bearing to the Ashanti king in West Africa. Kumasi’s splendor amazed the embassy. His eye-witness tale opened the land to white readers. The book is a classic of early faring-letters.
tob-10623-d1: William Hope Hodgson’s Carnacki the Ghost-Seeker strings the uncanny hunter’s eerie cases — the Horse Unseen, the Hog, the Thing Unseen, and more. His electric pentacle guards each haunted room. The tales blend dread, science, and sleight. The book is a classic of ghostly man-hunt stories.
tob-10626-d1: Nathaniel Hawthorne’s Mosses from an Old Manse strings his greatest tales — Young Goodman Brown, Rappaccini’s Daughter, the Birthmark, and more. The 1846 gathering shows his dark high mind at its height. The book is a cornerstone of American letters. Few gatherings cut so deep.
tob-10811-d1: Henry G. Ganss’s Martin Luther is the early 1900s Catholic life of the great German church-mender. The priest-storyteller handles Luther with keen fairness, neither graven image nor devil. The book gives Catholicism’s view of the church-sundering’s father. It matches the Protestant Lives.
tob-10887-d1: The St. Nicholas Play-and-Song Book — second number — strings bairns’ plays and song-plays from the beloved American bairns’ monthly. Parlors rang with these small productions. Young players found music, play, and glee herein. The book is a winsome keepsake of Edwardian childhood.
tob-10888-d1: Margaret Alice Murray’s Olden Egypt Tales retell the ageless Nile wonder-tales — Isis and Osiris, the world’s making, the underworld’s trials. Her tales keep the old gods alive. The Egypt-digger penned them for young readers. The book is a lightsome door to Egypt wonder-tales.
tob-10898-d1: Cornelius Mathews’s Indian Fairy Book retells the original legends of the North American Indians — brave heroes, cunning beasts, and great spirits. The 1868 collection brought native lore to American children. The book is a classic of American Indian folklore.
tob-10988-d1: E. Phillips Oppenheim’s Jacob’s Ladder is a thriller of intrigue, love, and high finance in the years before the Great War. The master of the Edwardian spy novel spins a tale of secret plots and daring. The book is vintage Oppenheim entertainment.
tob-11210-d1: Aleister Crowley’s Liber AL vel Legis — The Book of the Law — is the founding scripture of Thelema, received in Cairo in 1904. Its maxim is ‘Do what thou wilt.’ The book remains the central text of modern occultism.
tob-11338-d1: James Mooney’s Myths of the Cherokee — 1900 — gathers the sacred stories, folklore, and history of the Cherokee people. The great ethnologist’s monumental Bureau work preserves a nation’s heritage. No deeper record exists. The book is the classic source on Cherokee mythology.
tob-12905-d1: Martha Finley’s Elsie’s Vacation and After Events continues the beloved Elsie Dinsmore series — the pious heroine’s travels abroad and later life. Her wholesome adventures charmed generations of young readers. The series ran to twenty-eight volumes. The book is a classic of Victorian children’s fiction.
tob-12906-d1: Francis Cunningham’s The Pilot’s Daughter is a sea tale of the old sailing days — storms, shipwrecks, and a brave heroine’s courage. The novel captures the life of sailors aboard ship and ashore. The book is a sturdy piece of nautical fiction.
tob-12907-d1: Dorothy M. Richardson’s Deadlock is a volume of her Pilgrimage sequence — the pioneering stream-of-consciousness novels of English modernism. Miriam Henderson’s inner life unfolds moment by moment across its pages. Joyce learned from her example. The book is a landmark of modernist fiction.
tob-12908-d1: Rubén Darío’s Azul... — 1888 — is the book that launched Latin American modernismo, the great literary movement of the Spanish world. The Nicaraguan poet’s prose and verse dazzled readers everywhere. Its blue covers became a legend. The collection remains the movement’s founding text.
tob-12909-d1: This section of Mark Twain’s Adventures of Huckleberry Finn covers chapters 26 to the end — the Wilks fraud exposed, the feud’s aftermath, and Jim’s hard-won freedom. Huck’s voice carries the great American novel home. The chapters complete Twain’s masterpiece.
tob-12911-d1: Charles Darwin’s On the Origin of Species — 1859 — is the book that changed biology forever, setting out the theory of evolution by natural selection. Its careful argument reshaped science and human thought. The work remains the foundation of modern biology.
tob-12912-d1: Anton Chekhov’s The Duel and Other Stories gathers the Russian master’s finest tales — the duel, the ward, the steppe, the lady with the dog. His quiet irony revolutionized the modern short story. No one has written better short stories. The collection is essential Chekhov.
tob-12913-d1: Gustavus Myers’s Great Fortunes from Railroads exposes how the railroad barons built their empires — land grants, stock watering, bribery, and fraud. The muckraker’s history names names and follows the money. The book is a classic of American investigative writing.
tob-13137-d1: The Enchiridion of Epictetus — in Thomas Wentworth Higginson’s translation — is the Stoic handbook: short lessons on freedom and acceptance. The freed slave’s wisdom has guided readers for two thousand years. The book remains the essential Stoic manual. Its counsels fit in a pocket.
tob-13138-d1: This 1880s number of the Scientific American Supplement strings the week’s pieces on science, new tools, and trade. Engineers and tinkerers devoured it. The picture weekly bore fresh lore to its readers. The issue is a peep at the 1800s. Cuts show the wonders.
tob-13139-d1: Halbert Powers Gillette’s Concrete Construction: Methods and Costs is the engineer’s handbook of the reinforced-concrete age — how to build with the new wonder stuff. The 1908 volume taught a generation of builders. The book is a landmark of construction know-how. Its tables served the trade for decades.
tob-13140-d1: Stephen Leacock’s Moonbeams from the Larger Lunacy — 1915 — collects the great Canadian humorist’s satires on war, politics, and modern life. His gentle wit made him world-famous in his day. The book is a delight of early twentieth-century humor.
tob-13141-d1: Gustaf af Geijerstam’s Eksyksissä is a work of Finnish-language literature by the Swedish novelist. The title means ‘Lost’ or ‘Astray’ — a tale of wandering. The book preserves a distinctive voice from Nordic letters. Its pages await the curious reader.
tob-13143-d1: Walter Pater’s Appreciations, with an Essay on Style — 1889 — gathers the great aesthete’s critical essays on English literature. His famous essay on style remains a landmark of criticism. The book is essential for students of the Aesthetic movement.
tob-13144-d1: George Meredith’s The Amazing Marriage — 1895 — is a novel of love, pride, and high society in Victorian England. The master’s intricate style rewards patient readers. Its heroine is unforgettable. The book is a fine example of Meredith’s art.
tob-13145-d1: Caroline Frances Cornwallis’s book on Christian Sects in the 1800s musters the churches of her Victorian day — high, low, and broad. The writer’s fair tale is a prized time-capsule. The book serves church-story students. Her views are frank and fresh.
tob-13146-d1: James Freeman Clarke’s Ten Great Faiths — 1871 — musters the world’s high faiths: Hindu, Buddhist, Parsi, Christian, and more. The Boston preacher’s side-by-side tale was a first. The book stays a classic of god-lore. It opened Yankee eyes to Asia’s faiths.
tob-13147-d1: M. E. Durham’s Through the Land of the Serb recounts her intrepid travels in the early twentieth-century Balkans. The Englishwoman’s firsthand account illuminates Serbia and its neighbors. She knew the region like few outsiders. The book is a classic of Balkan travel writing.
tob-13148-d1: Clara Endicott Sears’s Bronson Alcott’s Fruitlands — 1915 — tells the story of the Transcendentalist commune in Harvard, Massachusetts. The 1843 experiment in utopian living failed within months. Louisa May Alcott lived there as a girl. The book is the classic account of the Fruitlands episode.
tob-13150-d1: This section of Mark Twain’s Adventures of Huckleberry Finn covers chapters 16 to 25 — the great raft journey, the Grangerford feud, and the Duke and Dauphin. Huck and Jim’s voyage deepens toward crisis. The chapters hold some of Twain’s finest writing.
tob-13151-d1: Arthur William Dunn’s Community Civics and Rural Life — 1919 — is a civics textbook written for country schools. The volume taught farm children their civic duties and community spirit. Its lessons shaped a generation. The book is a relic of progressive-era education.
tob-13152-d1: George Augustus Baker’s Point Lace and Diamonds — 1875 — is a society novel of Gilded Age New York. The tale of fashion, fortune, and ambition charmed its readers. Its ballroom scenes glitter. The book is a period piece of 1870s high life.
tob-13153-d1: The Junior Classics, Volume 4: Heroes and Heroines of Chivalry gathers stirring tales of knights and fair ladies for young readers. The anthology introduced generations of children to Arthur and Roland. Its pages ring with adventure. The book is a beloved children’s classic.
tob-13154-d1: The Works of John Dryden gather the poems, plays, and criticism of England’s first Poet Laureate. His satires, odes, and heroic plays defined the Augustan age of letters. Absalom and Achitophel crowns the verse. The collection is the monument of Restoration literature.
tob-13155-d1: Bill Nye’s Cordwood — 1887 — collects the humor of Edgar Wilson Nye, the beloved American funny man of the 1880s. His droll sketches delighted Gilded Age readers. His deadpan delivery was famous. The book is a classic of American humor.
tob-13322-d1: Randall Parrish’s Bob Hampton of Placer — 1906 — is a Western of the California mining camps. The tale of gold, guns, and grit follows the classic frontier formula. Parrish wrote dozens of such tales. The book is a rousing example of the early Western.
